payload.scope: People made the segmental-bronchus construct to name each airway branch that supplies a single bronchopulmonary segment, so that thoracic surgeons can resect discrete lung units and bronchoscopists can target individual segments.

definition.body: The segmental-bronchus is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps each airway branch supplying a single bronchopulmonary segment, arising as a division of the lobar bronchus. Parameters: (1) the generational position — each segmental bronchus branches from its parent lobar or main bronchus at approximately the 4th to 5th generation from the carina, with 10 on the right and 8 to 10 on the left; (2) the cartilaginous support — irregular hyaline cartilage plates persist in the wall, fewer than in the lobar generation but more than in the subsegmental, maintaining airway patency; (3) the epithelial lining — pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells, continuous with the lobar bronchial lining and transitioning distally toward simple cuboidal; (4) the segmental supply — each segmental bronchus supplies a discrete bronchopulmonary segment, a functionally independent unit of lung parenchyma with its own vascular supply; (5) the bronchoscopic reach — each segmental bronchus ostium is directly reachable by flexible bronchoscopy, making them the primary targets for segmental interventions. It persists as a maintained landmark in thoracic surgery, pulmonology, radiology, and anatomical teaching. e.g.: the segmental bronchus as described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition; segmental bronchus targeting for endobronchial valve placement in emphysema treatment; bronchopulmonary segmental anatomy in Shackelford's Surgery of the Esophagus and Thorax, 3rd edition | not: the lobar-bronchus (the larger branch from which segmental bronchi diverge, proximal structure); the subsegmental-bronchus (the smaller branch distal to the segmental bronchus, without a discrete parenchymal unit) [formal: bronchus segmentalis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

definition.body: The pulmonary lobule is a human-authored anatomical construct that partitions each pulmonary lobe into discrete pyramidal units with their apices directed toward the pleura. Parameters: (1) the boundary — the lobule is delimited by connective tissue septa extending from the visceral pleura into the lung parenchyma, dividing each lobe into approximately 50 to 100 lobules; (2) the central structure — a terminal bronchiole with its accompanying pulmonary artery branch runs through the center of the lobule, while lymphatics and veins occupy the peripheral septa; (3) the geometry — the lobule is pyramidal or polygonal in cross-section, approximately 1 to 2.5 cm in diameter, with its base toward the hilum and apex at the pleural surface; (4) the functional unit — each lobule is a self-contained ventilation and perfusion unit, with inflammatory patterns centered on the central bronchiole in diseases such as respiratory bronchiolitis and follicular bronchiolitis. It persists as a maintained landmark in pulmonary pathology, high-resolution CT interpretation, and anatomical teaching. e.g.: secondary pulmonary lobules visible as polygonal units on high-resolution CT; peribronchiolar granulomas in a sarcoidosis biopsy specimen; the wedge-shaped subpleural infarct of pulmonary thromboembolism | not: the pulmonary acinus (the finer gas-exchange unit nested inside a lobule); the pulmonary lobe (the larger organ division containing many lobules, bounded by fissures) [formal: lobulus pulmonis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.scope: People made the alveolar-capillary-membrane construct to identify the diffusion barrier between alveolar air and pulmonary capillary blood, so that physiologists can compute gas exchange and pathologists can assess thickening in disease.

definition.body: The alveolar-capillary membrane is a human-authored anatomical construct that delineates the barrier through which oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse between alveolar air and pulmonary capillary blood. Parameters: (1) the layered structure — the barrier comprises alveolar epithelium (type I pneumocyte), the fused basal lamina of epithelium and endothelium, and capillary endothelium; (2) the thickness — the thinnest point of the barrier measures 0.2 to 0.5 micrometers, a dimension critical to Fick diffusion, as measured by electron microscopy of human lung tissue; (3) the surface area — the gas-exchange surface spans approximately 70 square meters in the adult lung, partitioned into discrete alveolar-capillary units; (4) the clinical measure — thickening of the barrier from edema, fibrosis, or inflammation reduces diffusing capacity (DLCO), the standard noninvasive index of barrier integrity described in the ATS/ERS statement on respiratory function testing. payload.name: vital-capacity
payload.scope: People made the vital-capacity construct to measure the maximum volume of air a person can expel from the lungs after a maximal inhalation, so that clinicians can classify obstructive and restrictive ventilatory defects and track pulmonary disease progression.

definition.body: The vital-capacity is a human-authored physiological construct that quantifies the maximum volume of air that can be voluntarily exhaled from the lungs following a maximal inspiration. Parameters: (1) the measurement — vital capacity equals total lung capacity minus residual volume, obtained by spirometry as the difference between the peak inspiratory volume and the lowest achievable expiratory volume; (2) the reference equations — predicted normal values are calculated from age, height, sex, and ethnicity using standard reference equations such as those from the NHANES survey, with results expressed as a percentage of predicted; (3) the classification role — vital capacity below 80 percent predicted indicates restrictive ventilatory impairment when paired with reduced total lung capacity, and a reduced forced vital capacity combined with an elevated FEV1/FVC ratio confirms restriction per the ATS/ERS spirometry statement; (4) the clinical uses — vital capacity guides preoperative pulmonary risk assessment, monitors disease progression in neuromuscular disorders where values below one liter predict respiratory failure, and quantifies improvement after bronchodilator therapy. It persists as a maintained spirometric standard in clinical pulmonology, occupational medicine, and respiratory physiology. e.g.: ATS/ERS spirometry showing vital capacity of 2.8 liters at 32 percent predicted; NHANES reference equations calculating expected vital capacity for a 45-year-old male; the vital capacity of 0.8 liters predicting mechanical ventilation in Guillain-Barre syndrome | not: the total lung capacity (the larger volume including residual air that cannot be expelled); the residual volume (the air remaining after maximal exhalation, not part of vital capacity) [formal: capacitas vitalis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]
